title: Holy Grail
teaches: The Holy Grail as we trade it: a leader in a strong, young trend whose ADX pushed up and rose before the pullback makes its first touch of the rising 20-day EMA with the low holding over the 50-day, the buy is a market order as it trades over the prior day's high, the stop sits a few cents under the swing low the pullback just made, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest trailed on the 9 or 20 EMA, and a failed Grail closes that stock until it makes a new momentum high.

facts.quote: 1. The 14-period ADX must initially be greater than 30 and rising.
facts.claim: Raschke's rule 1: the 14-period ADX over 30 and rising at first, before the pullback.

facts.quote: 2. Look for a retracement in price to the 20 period exponential moving average. This will usually be accompanied by a turndown in the ADX.
facts.claim: Raschke's rule 2: a retracement to the 20-period exponential average, usually with the ADX turning down.

facts.quote: 3. When the price touches the 20 period moving average, put a buy stop above the high of the previous bar.
facts.claim: Raschke's rule 3: once price touches the average, a buy stop above the previous bar's high.

facts.quote: 4. Once filled, enter a protective sell stop at the newly formed swing low. Trail stops as profits grow.
facts.claim: Raschke's rule 4: the stop at the newly formed swing low; trail as profits grow.

facts.quote: Buy rules (sells are reversed)
facts.claim: Raschke: the buy rules are stated; sells are the reverse, so direction comes from the trend.

facts.quote: Therefore, any pullback from a new momentum high can be bought.
facts.claim: Raschke: a pullback from a new momentum high can be bought.

facts.quote: the majority of them have had Holy Grail patterns.
facts.claim: Raschke: most stocks that took part in the market's advance had Holy Grail patterns.

facts.quote: The 20 period exponential moving average often acts as support for stocks.
facts.claim: Raschke: the 20-period exponential average often acts as support.

facts.quote: This is a case where there is no reason to be in this trade.
facts.claim: Raschke's ETN lesson: a trade that does nothing is a trade with no reason to be in.

facts.quote: When you research this pattern, you should also look at cases when it fails.
facts.claim: Raschke: study the cases where the pattern fails.

facts.quote: The stock had a huge thrust up and pulled back nicely to the 20 period moving average. The ADX indicator was quite high.
facts.claim: Raschke's ETN example: a huge thrust, a nice pullback, a high ADX, and still no follow-through.

facts.quote: First, if a grail buy trade fails, I know I'm not going to look to buy pullbacks in that market.
facts.claim: Raschke: after a failed Grail she stops buying pullbacks in that market.

facts.quote: one that fails to hold the moving average.
facts.claim: Raschke defines a failed Grail as one that fails to hold the moving average.

facts.quote: in a trending market -- for Pete's sake, use market orders.
facts.claim: Raschke: in a trending market, use market orders.

facts.quote: I personally use a 20-period exponential moving average on all my markets.
facts.claim: Raschke uses a 20-period exponential moving average.

facts.quote: wait for the market to tip its hand and have that short-term momentum indicate what the market's going to do, and then wait for the first two- to three-day retracement to enter the market.
facts.claim: Raschke: momentum first, then the first two- to three-day retracement is the entry.

facts.quote: I avoid the markets where the ADX falls below 20 and is declining, because there's just not enough movement between the swings for me.
facts.claim: Raschke avoids markets where the ADX is under 20 and falling.

facts.quote: I use market orders most of the time.
facts.claim: Raschke uses market orders most of the time.

facts.quote: identify the up-trending stocks with the best relative strength at the beginning of a quarter.
facts.claim: Raschke picks up-trending stocks with the best relative strength.

facts.quote: In other words, I want to see only shallow retracements.
facts.claim: Raschke wants only shallow retracements.

facts.quote: I'm always looking at the swing highs or the swing lows.
facts.claim: Raschke reads stops and levels off the swing highs and swing lows.

facts.quote: The best setups will have confirming factors like the 3-10 oscillator making new momentum highs.
facts.claim: Raschke: the best setups have the 3-10 oscillator making new momentum highs.

facts.quote: By then you should be looking for a top.
facts.claim: Raschke: by the time the pullback shows up on the slowest time frames, look for a top.

facts.quote: 14-period ADX is initially above 30 and rising
facts.claim: Woods restates the filter: the 14-period ADX initially above 30 and rising.

facts.quote: Prices retrace down to 20-period simple moving average (SMA)
facts.claim: Woods describes the line as a 20-period simple average, not Raschke's exponential one.

facts.quote: First, a high ADX can mean that the trend is overdone and may reverse soon.
facts.claim: Woods' caution: a high ADX can mean the trend is overdone.

facts.quote: Second, gradual and protracted trends may unfold entirely without the ADX ever crossing above 30.
facts.claim: Woods' second caution: a slow, smooth trend may never push the ADX over 30.

facts.quote: Wilder suggests that a strong trend is present when ADX is above 25 and no trend is present when ADX is below 20.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: Wilder's strong-trend level is 25; under 20 there is no trend.

facts.quote: it can take around 150 periods of data to get true ADX values.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a true ADX value needs around 150 periods of history.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.
facts.claim: We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA: too stretched to buy.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part into a climax run.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: D38: A and B at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: Later sells are a judgment too: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.
facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the low, not exactly on it.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work
facts.claim: F68: after a correction, start with a few positions and add as they work.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: E56: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock.

facts.claim: A home-made ADX read 29.9 on a chop chart where the true Wilder ADX read 17.7.

facts.claim: Direction comes from price: the close above a rising 20 EMA on the ADX session; +DI over -DI is not a gate.

facts.claim: Length: 2 to 10 sessions from the momentum high to the touch.

facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.claim: Trail what is left: sell on a close below the 9 EMA. The 9 EMA, not the 20 EMA: a stock that has just pushed its ADX over 30 is usually moving fast.

questions.q: A leader just made a hard push to new highs and is now resting. Which line do you want it to pull back to for a Holy Grail?
questions.why: The 20 EMA. That's Raschke's line, and it's ours too. She uses a 20-period exponential average on all her markets. We draw the 9 and 20 EMA with the 50 and 200 SMA, so it's right there on your chart. The EMA leans on the latest closes, so it hugs a fast trend. The whole trade is a short first rest into it. The 50-day has a different job here. The dip should hold above it.
questions.lesson_line: The Grail rests on the 20 EMA. The 50-day is the floor under it.

wrong.The 20-day SMA: Some write-ups say simple. Raschke names the exponential average every time, and that's what we draw.
wrong.The 9 EMA: That's the faster line. A dip to the 9 is a tighter, different trade. The Grail rests to the 20.
wrong.The 50-day SMA: Too deep. The 50-day is the floor under the dip, not the line it rests on.

questions.simple: The 20 EMA. It's Raschke's line and ours, and a fast trend's first rest finds it.

reasons: Raschke's own words and the card agree

deeper.counter: Galen Woods' write-up of the setup says a 20-period simple average. Raschke named the exponential one every time she wrote her rules down, so we go with her.

questions.q: A stock's ADX reads 45 and rising. That tells you the stock is in a strong uptrend.
questions.why: False. A high ADX only tells you the trend is strong. It doesn't say which way. A stock falling hard has a high ADX too. So price gives you the direction. I want the close above a rising 20 EMA, the stock making higher highs. Then the ADX push tells me that uptrend has real force behind it. Raschke writes her buy rules and says sells are the reverse, for the same reason.
questions.lesson_line: The ADX says how hard. Price says which way.
questions.simple: False. The ADX shows how strong a trend is, not which way, and price tells you the direction.

questions.why: Just the A+. Orange means the market's under pressure, one step from Red. New buys fail more often when the market isn't backing them. So I only want my best idea, the cleanest rest with the tightest risk. The grade is our read on how clean a setup is, and the grade sets the size. The A and the B can wait for a better market. Green is when we press. Red is mostly cash.

Raschke starts the same way, with the up-trending stocks that have the best relative strength.

questions.simple: True. We want leaders with an RS rating of 80 or more, because the strongest stocks make the best pullback buys.

questions.q: Two stocks rest at their rising 20 EMA. One made a new high last week. The other last topped out three months ago. Which is the Grail?
choices: The one with last week's high
The one with the old high
Both, the line is the line
Neither until both make new highs
questions.answer: The one with last week's high
questions.why: The one with last week's high. The Grail is the first rest after fresh strength. In Raschke's words, any pullback from a new momentum high can be bought. A stock that topped months ago and drifts back to its line isn't resting after a push. It's just drifting. The push is what makes the first dip worth buying. Fresh push, first rest, that's the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Fresh strength first, then the rest. A stale high isn't momentum.

wrong.The one with the old high: That push is stale. Months of drifting isn't a rest, it's a stock losing steam.
wrong.Both, the line is the line: The line only matters after a fresh push. Without one, a touch is just a touch.
wrong.Neither until both make new highs: The first one already did. Last week's high is the fresh push you want.

questions.simple: The one with last week's high. The Grail buys the first rest after fresh strength, not a stale drift.

reasons: +3 the key rests on one cited fact (c03)
+2 rests on a card criterion still proposed, awaiting the owner (hg.momentum_high)
+1 fixed before (cold check 2026-11-10)

questions.q: A stock listed six weeks ago and its ADX already reads 40. That reading is as solid as one on a stock with years of history.
questions.why: False. The ADX is smoothed again and again, so it needs a long run of bars to settle. StockCharts' guide says it can take around 150 periods of data to get true ADX values. Six weeks of daily bars is nowhere near that. So on a fresh listing I don't lean on the ADX at all. And when you do read one, make sure it's the real Wilder ADX.
questions.lesson_line: A young chart's ADX is a guess. Give it history before you trust it.
questions.simple: False. The ADX needs a long history to settle, and six weeks of bars is nowhere near enough.

deeper.example: How it's worked out matters too. On one choppy chart, a home-made plain-sum ADX read 29.9 where the real Wilder ADX read 17.7. Wilder calls a strong trend above 25 and no trend below 20. Same chart, opposite answers.

choices: A Holy Grail, it closed back above

wrong.A Remount of the 50-day: A Remount loses the line for 5 or more straight closes, then buys it back. This was one dip, one day.

A normal pullback to the average is a big loss from your fill. At 7% the stretch is fine, so that one still gets judged on its chart. Funny thing is, a real Grail is almost never stretched. It just came back to its 20 EMA.

The longer it sits, the more that push fades. Weeks of chop is a base, and that's a different trade. So I count the days from the new high to the touch.

This was BAC in May 2006. Its low 20 sessions later sat 7.9% under the buy. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. A gap through it at the open has its own rule, but this one traded through during the day. So you're just out.

If it sets up at the 50-day later, that's a 50-day pullback with its own plan. Don't keep waiting on a trigger for a setup that already broke.
questions.lesson_line: The 50-day is the floor. Lose it before the trigger and the Grail is gone.

wrong.A buy at the 50-day: That's a different setup, the 50-day pullback, with its own rules. The Grail is gone.
wrong.Still live, give it time: Time doesn't fix it. It broke the 50-day before it ever triggered.
wrong.Live, the 20 EMA is rising: A rising line doesn't save it. It closed under the 50-day.

questions.simple: Gone. A close under the 50-day before the trigger means it's no longer a short rest.

questions.q: What setup is this?
choices: A Holy Grail, it retook the line
questions.why: A Remount. Count the closes under the line. Six straight under the 50-day is a stock that lost its line, not one resting on it. A Grail's dip holds above the 50-day the whole time. Lose the 50-day for 5 or more straight closes and buy it back, and you've got a Remount with its own plan. Name it right and the stop and size follow.
questions.lesson_line: Count the closes under the line. Five or more straight and it's a Remount.

wrong.A Holy Grail, it retook the line: A Grail's low never loses the 50-day. Six closes under it makes a Remount.
wrong.A plain 20 EMA pullback: It lost its 50-day for six closes. That's a far deeper break than a dip to the 20 EMA.
wrong.A 50-day pullback: A 50-day pullback rests on the line. This one lived under it for six closes, then took it back. That's the Remount.

questions.story: The stock closed under its 50-day for six straight sessions. Then it closed back over it on volume.
questions.simple: A Remount. Six straight closes under the 50-day is a lost line, and getting back over is the Remount.

deeper.trap: The trap is the close back over the line. It looks like a Grail holding, so count first. Five or more straight closes under the line, then a reclaim, is the Remount.

questions.q: Name the setup.

A Grail needs a rest all the way into the 20-day EMA, and this one never got there. Different line, different trade. Name the line it lost first, and the plan follows.
questions.lesson_line: Name the line it lost. The 4-day line is the Slingshot. The 20 EMA is the Grail.

wrong.An Oops reversal: An Oops is one day: open under the prior close and the prior low, then back over the close. This took four sessions.
wrong.A Holy Grail: The Grail needs a touch of the 20-day EMA. This one never got there.
wrong.A Remount: A Remount loses its 50-day or 200-day for 5 or more closes. This lost a 4-day line.

questions.simple: A Slingshot. It slipped under the 4-day line of the highs and came back, never touching the 20 EMA.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling every dip that recovers a Grail. Name the line first. Closes under the 4-day EMA of the highs that come back over make a Slingshot. A touch of the rising 20-day EMA, bought over the prior day's high, makes a Grail. Five or more closes under the 50-day or 200-day, then a reclaim, make a Remount.

questions.q: How should you have graded it going in?
choices: Lower, it was a slow rest
A+, a long rest builds power
questions.answer: Lower, it was a slow rest
questions.why: Lower than your best ones. Ten days is a long rest for a Grail, and the push the ADX measured had time to fade. A flag that takes that long has already lost its urgency. So it still trades, just graded down and sized down. The quick, orderly rests right after the push are the ones that grade up. And you grade it before the buy. A stop-out doesn't change what it looked like going in.

wrong.A+, every box was ticked: Boxes ticked isn't A+. Ten days is a slow rest.
wrong.A+, a long rest builds power: Backwards for a Grail. The longer it rests, the more the push fades.
wrong.Doesn't matter, it lost: It matters going in. The grade sets your size before you know the result.

questions.simple: Lower than your best. Ten days is a slow rest, the push had faded, so it gets less size.

deeper.trap: The trap is grading by the result. A loss feels like proof the setup was bad. But the grade sets the size, so it's fixed before the buy. Your journal records what happened after.

questions.q: Some web pages describe the Holy Grail with a 20-day simple average; Raschke names the exponential one.
questions.why: True. Woods writes a 20-period simple moving average; Raschke uses a 20-period exponential moving average. Our line is the 20-day EMA of closes.
questions.lesson_line: Follow the originator, not the rewrite. Exponential, every time.

questions.q: On the ADX session, what gives the trade its direction by our card?
choices: Price: the close above a rising 20 EMA
questions.answer: Price: the close above a rising 20 EMA
questions.why: Price. On the ADX session the close was above the 20 EMA, and the EMA is higher than 10 sessions earlier. +DI over -DI is not a gate.
questions.lesson_line: Strength from the ADX, direction from price. Keep the jobs separate.

wrong.+DI over -DI: A scanner's add-on, not Raschke's rule and not ours. Price decides direction.
wrong.The ADX itself: The ADX measures strength; a strong downtrend also has a high ADX.
wrong.The 50-day's slope: The 50-day is the floor under the touch. The 20 EMA and the close give direction.

questions.q: Sell, hold or add on this leg?
choices: Sell a big part into it
Hold it all, let it run
questions.answer: Sell a big part into it
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. That's the move you held for. A vertical leg on your own long is strength you sell into, before it snaps back. How much is your call. I'll sell a big chunk and trail the rest on the 9 EMA. This was LITE in July 2025, and this kind of leg started right after its 3R. Don't add here. A vertical leg is where you sell, not where you buy more.
questions.lesson_line: Into a vertical leg, sell a big part. How much is your call.

wrong.Hold it all, let it run: A climax is the strength we sell into. Hold it all and you give a lot back.
wrong.Sell all of it at 5R: 5R isn't an exit. Sell a big part and trail the rest.
wrong.Add shares, it's strong: Never add into a vertical leg. That's where you sell.

questions.story: You bought at 91.78 with the stop at 88.88 on the trigger. It hits 3R in five sessions and you hold. Then a parabolic leg carries it well past 5R, and it goes vertical.
questions.simple: Sell a big part into it. A climax run is strength to sell into, and how much is your call.

deeper.trap: Adding because the leg looks strong. The plan is one entry at one price. A vertical leg is where you sell, not where you buy more.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.why: 200. No longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. The touch session closes above it, or it is no trade.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day first. Then look at the line.
questions.sentence: No Holy Grail long below the ___-day simple moving average.

questions.q: The honest stop is 5.5% away. What do you do?
choices: Skip the stop and watch it
questions.why: Wait for a tighter trigger. 5.5% is past the 5% I'll accept. I like 1 to 3%, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% I'll take. Past that, I mostly wait for a spot where the low of the day, the LOD, puts my stop inside 5%. What you never do is drag the stop up to 3% so the size fits. Then it sits inside the dip, in the noise, not where the setup is wrong. You'd get shaken out of a trade that was fine.
questions.lesson_line: Never back-fit a stop. Past 5%, wait for a tighter trigger.

wrong.Wait for a tighter trigger: Waiting is fine. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger rather than take the trade.
wrong.Move the stop up to 3%: Now the stop sits in the noise, not where the setup is wrong. You get shaken out of a good trade.
wrong.Full size, it's one trade: Full size on a 5.5% stop blows past the risk you planned.
wrong.Skip the stop and watch it: Every position gets a real stop with the broker. No exceptions.

questions.story: A Grail sets up and you plan to buy the trigger. The swing low sits 5.5% under your planned entry.
questions.simple: Wait for a tighter trigger. Past 5% we mostly wait, and we never drag the stop up to fit.

deeper.trap: The trap is forcing the trade. When the honest stop is past 5%, the fix is never a tighter stop. A stop raised inside the swing low no longer marks where the setup is wrong. Most of the time you wait, and another trigger with a closer low of the day comes along.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 9)

questions.q: Which grades higher, and is volume a gate?
choices: The quiet one; a plus, not a gate
The loud one; buyers are back
Neither; both fail a volume gate
questions.answer: The quiet one; a plus, not a gate
questions.why: The quiet one grades up, and volume is not a gate. Our scan found a quiet pullback did not change much (27.6% against 26.7%), so it is a plus only.
questions.lesson_line: Light volume into the line is a nice touch. It is not the trade.

wrong.The loud one; buyers are back: Heavy volume on a pullback is selling, not buying. It grades down, a little.
wrong.Neither; both fail a volume gate: There is no volume gate. No source requires one.

questions.q: A home-made ADX on a short window can read a trend where the true Wilder ADX reads chop.
questions.why: True. A plain-sum ADX read 29.9 on a chop chart where the Wilder ADX read 17.7. True ADX values take around 150 periods of data.
questions.lesson_line: Check which ADX you are reading before you trust the number.

questions.q: Do you take the trigger?
choices: Yes, a clean setup is a setup
No, but only the $7 price fails
questions.why: No. We trade stocks at $10 or more that do at least $20 million a day. This one is $7 and does about $4 million. It fails both. A thin stock can gap through your stop on nothing. When you need out, there's nobody to sell to. A pretty chart doesn't fix that. Stocks this thin shouldn't even be on your watch list.
questions.lesson_line: A clean touch in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes, a clean setup is a setup: The setup's fine, the stock isn't ours. Liquidity comes before the chart.
wrong.Yes, at half size: Smaller size doesn't make a thin stock liquid. It's no trade.
wrong.No, but only the $7 price fails: It fails twice. About $4 million a day is under the $20 million floor too.

questions.story: A clean first touch of the 20 EMA on a $7 stock. It trades about $4 million a day.
questions.simple: No. It's under $10 and under $20 million a day, too thin to get in and out clean.

deeper.trap: The trap is a perfect chart. Liquidity comes first: $10 or more, and $20 million a day. A stock under either line isn't one we trade, however clean it looks.

questions.q: The highest close of the last 20 sessions printed 7 sessions ago; the touch is today. Does the test pass?
choices: No; it must be within 5 sessions
No; it must be a 52-week high
questions.why: Yes. The highest close of the last 20 sessions was made within the 10 sessions before the touch. Seven is inside ten.
questions.lesson_line: Count back from the touch. Ten sessions is the window for the high.

wrong.No; it must be within 5 sessions: The window is 10 sessions, not 5. The A+ length is a different row.
wrong.No; it must be a 52-week high: A 20-session closing high is the test. A 52-week high is not required.

questions.q: By our rules, what came off on the way up?
choices: A third at 3R and a third at 5R
questions.answer: A third at 3R and a third at 5R
questions.why: Two thirds banked. A third at 3R, a third at 5R, stop at breakeven, the last third on the 10-day trail. CI reached 3R in 2 sessions and ran to 12.9R.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. The trims are what you keep when the run ends.

wrong.Nothing; it had not reached 10R: Waiting for 10R with nothing banked is how a winner becomes a scratch.
wrong.All of it at 5R: The last third rides the trail. 5R is the second trim, not the exit.

questions.story: Bought at 36.72, stop 36.03, the morning after a first touch. It reaches 3R in two sessions and keeps going for weeks.

questions.q: How many do you take today?
choices: A few of the best ones
All seven, Green is full risk
One, and add to it later
questions.answer: A few of the best ones
questions.why: A few of the best ones. The first Green day after a correction can be a head fake. Buy all seven, the turn fails, and seven stops hit at once. Start with a few. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you open more. If they fail, you lost a little and you're mostly in cash. Each one still goes on at full size, one price, one stop. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: Green after a correction: a few first. Let the market earn your exposure.

wrong.All seven, Green is full risk: Full risk is where Green can take you, not day one. If the turn fails, seven stops hit at once.
wrong.None, wait a week: Waiting a week isn't the plan. Start with a few and let them tell you.
wrong.One, and add to it later: An add is never the plan. More exposure means more positions, each at full size.

questions.story: After a correction, the market filter just turned Green. Seven leaders on your list trigger today off a first touch of the 20 EMA.
questions.simple: A few of the best. The first Green day can be a fake, so let the first ones work before opening more.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading add as they work as adding shares. It means more positions. Start with a few, then open more as the first ones work. Each one still goes on at full size, at one price, with one stop.

questions.q: What's your plan for the stop and the first sell?
choices: Under swing low, judge the sell
1 ATR under low, judge the sell
Under swing low, a third at 3R
1 ATR under low, a third at 3R
questions.answer: Under swing low, judge the sell
questions.why: A few cents under the swing low, and you judge the first sell. The swing low is the lowest low from the touch through your buy day. If that breaks, the rest failed. A full ATR under it just adds risk. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. This was EXPD in March 2006, the first two- to three-day retracement Raschke talks about. It reached 3R in three sessions. A third sold right there would have left most of the move on the table.
questions.lesson_line: Market entry, a stop a few cents under the swing low, a first sell you judge.

wrong.1 ATR under low, judge the sell: The sell is right. A stop a full ATR under the low just adds risk. Ours sits a few cents under it.
wrong.Under swing low, a third at 3R: The stop is right. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
wrong.1 ATR under low, a third at 3R: Two misses. The stop is too wide, and the first sell isn't a fixed third.

questions.story: A three-day, 3.6% rest into the 20 EMA after a fresh high. Tomorrow morning it trades over today's high and you buy at market.
questions.simple: A few cents under the swing low, and a first sell you judge, not a fixed third at 3R.

deeper.example: Raschke's own rule is a buy stop above the previous bar's high. We buy everything at market, so we buy as it trades over the prior day's high. Raschke says the same about a trending market: use market orders.

questions.q: This is the touch day. Green market, RS 80 or more, a first rest into the rising 20 EMA after a hard push. What's the play?
choices: Buy it here at the close
questions.why: Buy it on the trigger, tomorrow, as it trades over today's high. Check the chart first. The dip's low held above the 50-day, and price sits well above the 200-day. Seven quiet red days drifted into the line, no panic. That's a clean rest. You don't buy the touch itself. You wait for it to trade over today's high, because that's your proof buyers showed up. This was CI in October 2000. It triggered the next morning and never looked back.
questions.lesson_line: First rest, low over the 50, price over the 200. Then wait for the trigger.

wrong.Pass, it broke the 50-day: Look again. The low held above the 50-day.
wrong.Pass, it's under the 200-day: It's well above the 200-day. The location checks out.
wrong.Buy it here at the close: Buying the touch is the mistake. We buy through the trigger, never the close.

questions.simple: Buy on tomorrow's trigger. The low held over the 50-day and price sits above the 200-day.

deeper.trap: Seven red days into the line can look like weakness. Check what matters: the low over the 50-day and price over the 200-day. Then wait for the trigger. Buying the touch itself is the mistake.

wrong.Yes, the ADX is strong: The ADX says how strong, not where. Under the 200-day is a no, whatever the ADX.

questions.why: False. You hold through a report only when the trade is up 5R. At 2R it's not, so it comes off before the report. A report can gap a stock way past your stop. At 5R you've got enough cushion to sit through that. At 2R you don't, even with the stop at breakeven, because a stop can't catch a gap.
questions.lesson_line: Hold through a report only at 5R or more. At 2R, it comes off first.
questions.simple: False. We hold through a report only at 5R or more, and 2R isn't enough cushion.

deeper.trap: The trap is feeling safe at 2R with the stop at breakeven. A gap on the report doesn't care where your stop is. Only a trade up 5R stays on through a report.

questions.q: What's this one called?
questions.why: An Oops. It opened under yesterday's close, traded under yesterday's low, and won the close back the same day. That's sellers getting caught in one session. A Grail needs a rest into the 20 EMA first, and this one never touched it. A U&R undercuts a level everyone can see, a real swing low or range low. Yesterday's low here was neither. A Slingshot takes 3 to 7 closes under the 4-day EMA of the highs.
questions.lesson_line: One day's open-and-reclaim is the Oops. A rest to the 20 EMA and a push over the high is the Grail.

wrong.A Holy Grail: It never touched its 20 EMA, so there's no Grail. The Grail is bought after a touch of the line.
wrong.A swing-low U&R: A U&R undercuts a level everyone can see, like a swing low or range low. Yesterday's low was neither.
wrong.A Slingshot: A Slingshot needs 3 to 7 closes under the 4-day EMA of the highs, then a close back over. Nothing here shows that.

questions.story: The stock opens under yesterday's close and trades under yesterday's low. By the bell it has won back yesterday's close. Yesterday's low wasn't a swing low or a range low. It never touched its 20 EMA.
questions.simple: An Oops. It opened under yesterday's close, dipped under yesterday's low and won the close back that day.

deeper.counter: A lot of dips that recover look alike, so name the level that was lost and how long it took. One day under yesterday's low, back over yesterday's close, is the Oops. A dip under a level everyone can see, won back within 3 sessions, is the U&R. A touch of the rising 20 EMA, then a trade over the prior day's high, is the Grail.

questions.q: A one-session dip to the 20 EMA that bounces the next day counts as a Holy Grail pullback.
questions.why: False. Length is 2 to 10 sessions from the momentum high to the touch. Raschke's first retracement was two to three days; one day is a wobble, not a rest.
questions.lesson_line: A rest has to last long enough to shake someone out. One day does not.

questions.q: Where's Wednesday's trigger?
choices: No trigger, the lower low ends it
questions.why: Just over 52.00, Tuesday's high. Raschke's buy stop sits above the high of the previous bar. Tuesday is now the previous bar, so the trigger drops to just over 52.00. Leave it at 52.40 and you buy later and higher, with more distance to your stop. A lower low by itself doesn't kill it. When price trades over 52.00, you buy at market. Your stop goes a few cents under the new swing low.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger follows the latest high down.

wrong.Over 52.40, Monday's high: Monday's level is stale. The trigger follows the latest day's high.
wrong.Buy at the 20 EMA touch: Buying the touch instead of the trigger is the mistake. You wait for a trade over the latest high.
wrong.No trigger, the lower low ends it: A lower low alone doesn't end it. The trigger just rolls down to Tuesday's high.

If Wednesday also makes a lower low with no trigger, it rolls again to Wednesday's high. Keep an eye on the 50-day while it does.

questions.story: You hold what's left of a Holy Grail winner on your trail. Then it goes vertical: three straight up days, the last two on overnight gap ups. Ranges widen and volume rises each day.
questions.q: What do you do with what's left?
choices: Sell a big part into the strength
Hold it until the trail sells it
Lower the stop to give it room
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the strength
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. That's a parabolic burst on your own long. Three straight up days, two straight gap ups, wider ranges, rising volume. The more of those boxes it checks, the stronger the signal, and this one checks most. Don't wait for the trail to sell it for you. By the time a burst closes under the 9 EMA, you've given back a big chunk. How much you sell is your call. Keep a piece and trail it.
questions.lesson_line: A burst on your own long is strength to sell into. How much is your call.

wrong.Hold it until the trail sells it: The trail is the default exit. A climax run gets sold into first, a big part, by judgment.
wrong.Add shares while it's strong: Never add into a burst. It's strength you sell into.
wrong.Lower the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into the burst. Waiting for the trail hands back a big chunk of the move.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, and B26's reading of Bracco's burst)
